```{r}
set.seed(100)
```

## Hypothesis Test for Difference of Means (Two-Tailed, Equal Variance)

::: {.callout title="Theorem 27.1"}
Let $X_{11}, X_{12}, \dots, X_{1n_1}$ be independent, normally distributed random variables with mean $\mu_1$ and unknown standard deviation $\sigma$ and let $X_{21}, X_{22}, \dots, X_{2n_2}$ be independent, normally distributed random variables with mean $\mu_2$ and unknown standard deviation $\sigma$. Consider the test $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$ vs $H_A: \mu_1 \neq \mu_2$. If we want the Type-I error rate to be no larger than $\alpha$. Then we would reject $H_0$ when the following was true:

$$
\left|\frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}} \right| > t_{n_1+n_2-2, 1-\alpha/2}
$$

where

$$
s_p = \sqrt{\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2 + (n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}}
$$

If the data are non-normal, but $n_1, n_2$ are sufficiently large, then this is an approximate $100 \times (1-\alpha)\%$ interval.
:::

A rule of thumb for determining equal variance is that $\max(s_1^2, s_2^2) \leq 4 \times \min(s_1^2, s_2^2)$

## Hypothesis Test for Difference of Means (Left-Tailed, Equal Variance)

::: {.callout title="Theorem 27.2"}
Let $X_{11}, X_{12}, \dots, X_{1n_1}$ be independent, normally distributed random variables with mean $\mu_1$ and unknown standard deviation $\sigma$ and let $X_{21}, X_{22}, \dots, X_{2n_2}$ be independent, normally distributed random variables with mean $\mu_2$ and unknown standard deviation $\sigma$. Consider the test $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$ vs $H_A: \mu_1 < \mu_2$. If we want the Type-I error rate to be no larger than $\alpha$. Then we would reject $H_0$ when the following was true:

$$
\frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}} < t_{n_1+n_2-2, \alpha}
$$
:::

## Hypothesis Test for Difference of Means (Right-Tailed, Equal Variance)

::: {.callout title="Theorem 27.3"}
Let $X_{11}, X_{12}, \dots, X_{1n_1}$ be independent, normally distributed random variables with mean $\mu_1$ and unknown standard deviation $\sigma$ and let $X_{21}, X_{22}, \dots, X_{2n_2}$ be independent, normally distributed random variables with mean $\mu_2$ and unknown standard deviation $\sigma$. Consider the test $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$ vs $H_A: \mu_1 > \mu_2$. If we want the Type-I error rate to be no larger than $\alpha$. Then we would reject $H_0$ when the following was true:

$$
\frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}} > t_{n_1+n_2-2, 1-\alpha}
$$
:::

## P-Value for Test for Difference of Means (Two-Tailed, Equal Variance)

For a two-tailed test for the difference of population means ($H_A: \mu_1 \neq \mu_2$), the p-value would be computed as follows:

$$
P\left(\frac{\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2}{S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}} \geq \left|\frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}}\right| \Bigg| \mu_1 = \mu_2\right)
$$

## P-Value for Test for Difference of Means (Left-Tailed, Equal Variance)

For a left-tailed test for the difference of population means ($H_A: \mu_1 < \mu_2$), the p-value would be computed as follows:

$$
P\left(\frac{\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2}{S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}} \leq \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}} \Bigg| \mu_1 = \mu_2\right)
$$

## P-Value for Test for Difference of Means (Right-Tailed, Equal Variance)

For a right-tailed test for the difference of population means ($H_A: \mu_1 < \mu_2$), the p-value would be computed as follows:

$$
P\left(\frac{\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2}{S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}} \geq \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}} \Bigg| \mu_1 = \mu_2\right)
$$

## Ex: Drug Study

::: {.callout title="Example 27.1"}
You are comparing two drugs to see how effective they are in reducing blood pressure. First, you get a baseline blood pressure measurement for everyone in the study. You then randomly assign 35 patients to receive drug A and 35 patients to receive drug B. After two weeks, you record the reduction in blood pressure from the baseline and find that $\bar{x}_A = -5$, $\bar{x}_B = -3$, $s_A^2 = 10$, and $s_B^2 = 14$.

Conduct a hypothesis test at the 5% significance level to test if the true difference in means is different than 0 where the difference is defined as drug A minus drug B.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
xbar_A <- -5; xbar_B <- -3
s2_A <- 10; s2_B <- 14
n_A <- 35; n_B <- 35
alpha <- 0.05

sp <- sqrt(((n_A-1)*s2_A + (n_B-1)*s2_B)/(n_A + n_B - 2))
t_statistic <- (xbar_A-xbar_B)/(sp*sqrt(1/n_A + 1/n_B))

cat("The t-statistic is: ", t_statistic, ", the critical value is: ", qt(1-alpha/2, n_A + n_B - 2), ", and the p-value is: ", 2*pt(-abs(t_statistic), n_A + n_B - 2), sep = "")
```

## Ex: Weight Loss

::: {.callout title="Example 27.2"}
A nutritionist is studying the effects of two different diets on weight loss. Two independent groups of participants are assigned, 40 to Diet A and 50 to Diet B. After 8 weeks, the weight change (in pounds) from the start of the study is recorded. The results show that for Diet A, $\bar{x}_A = -8$, $s_A^2 = 16$ and for Diet B, $\bar{x}_B = -6$, $s_B^2 = 20$.

Conduct a hypothesis test at the 1% significance level to test if the true difference in means is less than 0 where the difference is defined as diet A minus diet B.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
xbar_A <- -8; xbar_B <- -6
s2_A <- 16; s2_B <- 20
n_A <- 40; n_B <- 50
alpha <- 0.01

sp <- sqrt(((n_A-1)*s2_A + (n_B-1)*s2_B)/(n_A + n_B - 2))
t_statistic <- (xbar_A-xbar_B)/(sp*sqrt(1/n_A + 1/n_B))

cat("The t-statistic is: ", t_statistic, ", the critical value is: ", qt(alpha, n_A + n_B - 2), ", and the p-value is: ", pt(t_statistic, n_A + n_B - 2), sep = "")
```

## Ex: Teaching

::: {.callout title="Example 27.3"}
A researcher is analyzing two different teaching methods to see which one leads to better test scores. Two independent groups of students are randomly assigned to Method A or Method B (38 to method A and 44 to method B). At the end of the semester, the final exam scores are recorded. The results show that for Method A, $\bar{x}_A = 82$, $s_A^2 = 25$, and for Method B, $\bar{x}_B = 78$, $s_B^2 = 30$.

Conduct a hypothesis test at the 5% significance level to test if the true difference in means is greater than 0 where the difference is defined as method A minus method B.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
xbar_A <- 82; xbar_B <- 78
s2_A <- 25; s2_B <- 30
n_A <- 38; n_B <- 44
alpha <- 0.05

sp <- sqrt(((n_A-1)*s2_A + (n_B-1)*s2_B)/(n_A + n_B - 2))
t_statistic <- (xbar_A-xbar_B)/(sp*sqrt(1/n_A + 1/n_B))

cat("The t-statistic is: ", t_statistic, ", the critical value is: ", qt(1-alpha, n_A + n_B - 2), ", and the p-value is: ", 1-pt(t_statistic, n_A + n_B - 2), sep = "")
```

## Ex: Fuel

::: {.callout title="Example 27.4"}
You are investigating two different types of additives for engine oil lubricants, call them Additive A and Additive B. Scientists have 40 tests with Additive A and 45 tests with Additive B and recorded the fuel efficiency (in mpg) for each test, which can be found below:

```{r, echo = TRUE}
fuel_A <- c(32, 31, 29.7, 28.3, 30.3, 27.3, 31.4, 28.8, 28.9, 30.9, 30, 31,
            34.8, 31.1, 32.7, 29.4, 27.8, 33.3, 27.8, 22, 31.9, 37.1, 26,
            30.9, 28.8, 35, 32.1, 28.9, 24, 26, 33.6, 32.7, 35.4, 34, 34.7,
            27.7, 26.9, 29.7, 25.8, 33.8)

fuel_B <- c(26.2, 27.7, 26.2, 26.2, 25.1, 24.2, 29.3, 23.4, 24.5, 25.9,
            31.3, 25.1, 29, 25.5, 27.8, 25.5, 30.2, 28.2, 28.8, 25.1,
            24.3, 26.6, 28.2, 29.7, 33.6, 30.1, 24.5, 25.8, 25.9, 31,
            27.7, 31, 30.7, 31.1, 21.8, 21.6, 25.6, 23.1, 30.5, 27.6,
            25.2, 32.4, 31.9, 30.3, 29.6)
```

Conduct a hypothesis test at the 1% significance level to test if the true difference in means is different from 0 where difference is defined as Additive B minus Additive A
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
t.test(fuel_B, fuel_A, alternative = "two.sided", 
       var.equal = TRUE, conf.level = 0.99)$p.value
```

## Hypothesis Test for Difference of Means (Two-Tailed, Unequal Variance)

::: {.callout title="Theorem 27.4"}
Let $X_{11}, X_{12}, \dots, X_{1n_1}$ be independent, normally distributed random variables with mean $\mu_1$ and unknown variance $\sigma_1^2$ and let $X_{21}, X_{22}, \dots, X_{2n_2}$ be independent, normally distributed random variables with mean $\mu_2$ and unknown variance $\sigma_2^2$. Consider the test $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$ vs $H_A: \mu_1 \neq \mu_2$. If we want the Type-I error rate to be no larger than $\alpha$. Then we would reject $H_0$ when the following was true:

$$
\left|\frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}} \right| > t_{df, 1-\alpha/2}
$$

where

$$
df = \frac{\left(\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}\right)^2}{\frac{s_1^4/n_1^2}{n_1-1} + \frac{s_2^4/n_2^2}{n_2-1}}
$$
:::

A rule of thumb for determining equal variance is that $\max(s_1^2, s_2^2) \leq 4 \times \min(s_1^2, s_2^2)$

## Hypothesis Test for Difference of Means (Left-Tailed, Unequal Variance)

::: {.callout title="Theorem 27.5"}
Let $X_{11}, X_{12}, \dots, X_{1n_1}$ be independent, normally distributed random variables with mean $\mu_1$ and unknown variance $\sigma_1^2$ and let $X_{21}, X_{22}, \dots, X_{2n_2}$ be independent, normally distributed random variables with mean $\mu_2$ and unknown variance $\sigma_2^2$. Consider the test $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$ vs $H_A: \mu_1 < \mu_2$. If we want the Type-I error rate to be no larger than $\alpha$. Then we would reject $H_0$ when the following was true:

$$
\frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}} < t_{df, \alpha}
$$
:::

## Hypothesis Test for Difference of Means (Right-Tailed, Unequal Variance)

::: {.callout title="Theorem 27.6"}
Let $X_{11}, X_{12}, \dots, X_{1n_1}$ be independent, normally distributed random variables with mean $\mu_1$ and unknown variance $\sigma_1^2$ and let $X_{21}, X_{22}, \dots, X_{2n_2}$ be independent, normally distributed random variables with mean $\mu_2$ and unknown variance $\sigma_2^2$. Consider the test $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$ vs $H_A: \mu_1 > \mu_2$. If we want the Type-I error rate to be no larger than $\alpha$. Then we would reject $H_0$ when the following was true:

$$
\frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}} > t_{df, 1-\alpha}
$$
:::

## P-Value for Test for Difference of Means (Two-Tailed, Unequal Variance)

For a two-tailed test for the difference of population means ($H_A: \mu_1 \neq \mu_2$), the p-value would be computed as follows:

$$
P\left(\frac{\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2}{\sqrt{\frac{S_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{S_2^2}{n_2}}} \geq \left|\frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}}\right| \Bigg| \mu_1 = \mu_2\right)
$$

## P-Value for Test for Difference of Means (Left-Tailed, Unequal Variance)

For a left-tailed test for the difference of population means ($H_A: \mu_1 < \mu_2$), the p-value would be computed as follows:

$$
P\left(\frac{\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2}{\sqrt{\frac{S_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{S_2^2}{n_2}}} \leq \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}} \Bigg| \mu_1 = \mu_2\right)
$$

## P-Value for Test for Difference of Means (Right-Tailed, Equal Variance)

For a right-tailed test for the difference of population means ($H_A: \mu_1 > \mu_2$), the p-value would be computed as follows:

$$
P\left(\frac{\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2}{\sqrt{\frac{S_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{S_2^2}{n_2}}} \geq \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}} \Bigg| \mu_1 = \mu_2\right)
$$

## Ex: CV

::: {.callout title="Example 27.7"}
A team of researchers is investigating whether a new image classification algorithm (algorithm A) has a lower average error rate than a traditional algorithm (algorithm B). They evaluate both algorithms on separate sets of images, with 45 images processed by the traditional algorithm and 38 images processed by the new algorithm. The traditional algorithm has an average error rate of 12.5% with a sample variance of 36%, while the new algorithm has an average error rate of 11.3% with a sample variance of 8%. Perform a hypothesis test at the 10% significance level to test this hypothesis.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
xbar_A <- 11.3; xbar_B <- 12.5
s2_A <- 8; s2_B <- 36
n_A <- 38; n_B <- 45
alpha <- 0.1

t_statistic <- (xbar_A - xbar_B) / sqrt((s2_A / n_A) + (s2_B / n_B))
df <- ((s2_A / n_A + s2_B / n_B)^2) / (((s2_A / n_A)^2 / (n_A - 1)) + ((s2_B / n_B)^2 / (n_B - 1)))

cat("Test Statistic:", t_statistic, ", Critical Value:", qt(alpha, df), ", P-Value:", pt(t_statistic, df))
```

## Ex: GPU

::: {.callout title="Example 27.8"}
A hardware review team is investigating whether the average frame rate of a new GPU (GPU A) differs from that of an established GPU (GPU B) when running a popular video game. They test GPU B on 40 gaming sessions and GPU A on 35 gaming sessions. GPU B achieves an average frame rate of 75 frames per second (fps) with a sample variance of 64, while GPU A achieves an average frame rate of 78 fps with a sample variance of 12. Perform a hypothesis test at the 5% significance level to test whether there is a difference in average frame rates between the two GPUs.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
xbar_A <- 78; xbar_B <- 75
s2_A <- 12; s2_B <- 64
n_A <- 35; n_B <- 40
alpha <- 0.05

t_statistic <- (xbar_A - xbar_B) / sqrt((s2_A / n_A) + (s2_B / n_B))
df <- ((s2_A / n_A + s2_B / n_B)^2) / (((s2_A / n_A)^2 / (n_A - 1)) + ((s2_B / n_B)^2 / (n_B - 1)))

cat("Test Statistic:", t_statistic, ", Critical Value:", qt(1-alpha/2, df), ", P-Value:", 2*pt(-abs(t_statistic), df))
```

## Ex: Fertilizer

::: {.callout title="Example 27.9"}
An ecologist is studying whether a new fertilizer increases the average height of a particular plant species. In a controlled experiment, they apply the fertilizer to one group of 50 plants and leave another group of 48 plants untreated. The untreated plants have an average height of 30.2 cm with a sample variance of 25, while the treated plants have an average height of 33.1 cm with a sample variance of 110. Perform a hypothesis test at the 1% significance level to test whether the fertilizer increases the average height of the plants.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
xbar_A <- 33.1; xbar_B <- 30.2
s2_A <- 110; s2_B <- 25
n_A <- 50; n_B <- 48
alpha <- 0.01

t_statistic <- (xbar_A - xbar_B) / sqrt((s2_A / n_A) + (s2_B / n_B))
df <- ((s2_A / n_A + s2_B / n_B)^2) / (((s2_A / n_A)^2 / (n_A - 1)) + ((s2_B / n_B)^2 / (n_B - 1)))

cat("Test Statistic:", t_statistic, ", Critical Value:", qt(1-alpha, df), ", P-Value:", 1-pt(t_statistic, df))
```

## Ex: Novels

::: {.callout title="Example 27.10"}
A literary researcher is investigating whether contemporary novels have a lower average sentence length compared to classic novels. To study this, the researcher selects a random sample of 35 classic novels and 40 contemporary novels. Use the data below to perform a hypothesis test to test this hypothesis at the 5% significance level.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
contemp <- c(12, 12, 10, 12, 13, 13, 11, 14, 11, 13, 17, 10, 13, 8, 10, 13, 11, 10, 
             10, 13, 9, 10, 13, 13, 14, 8, 9, 13, 15, 11, 11, 13, 13, 12, 9)

classic <- c(15, 10, 24, 14, 12, 13, 25, 5, 20, 4, 4, 17, 13, 26, 11, 7, 8, 17, 15, 13, 14, 12,
             13, 17, 13, 7, 16, 15, 15, 28, 16, 16, 31, 14, 5, 17, 8, 15, 16, 23)
```
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
max(var(contemp), var(classic)) <= 4*min(var(contemp), var(classic))
t.test(contemp, classic, alternative = "less", var.equal = FALSE, conf.level = 0.95)$p.value
t.test(classic, contemp, alternative = "greater", var.equal = FALSE, conf.level = 0.95)$p.value
```

## Ex: Tax

::: {.callout title="Example 27.11"}
An economist is studying whether two different tax policies result in different average levels of consumer spending (in thousands of dollars). To investigate this, the economist collects a random sample of households from regions that have implemented Policy A and another sample from regions that have implemented Policy B. Use the data below to perform a hypothesis test at the 10% significance level to determine if there is a difference in average consumer spending between the two policies.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
policy_A <- c(9, 10, 16, 12, 14, 18, 15, 12, 13, 14, 11, 13, 14, 19, 11, 19, 16, 14, 16, 
              23, 9, 13, 15, 12, 16, 15, 12, 15, 13, 13, 11, 11, 17, 13, 21)
policy_B <- c(23, 22, 30, 20, 11, 16, 9, 18, 12, 5, 20, 10, 20, 17, 17, 16, 22, 8, 13,
              11, 7, 12, 31, 17, 18, 14, 13, 29, 25, 12, 6, 20, 20, 16, 14)
```
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
max(var(policy_A), var(policy_B)) <= 4*min(var(policy_A), var(policy_B))
t.test(policy_A, policy_B, alternative = "two.sided", var.equal = FALSE, conf.level = 0.9)$p.value
t.test(policy_B, policy_A, alternative = "two.sided", var.equal = FALSE, conf.level = 0.9)$p.value
```

## Ex: Load Times

::: {.callout title="Example 27.12"}
A tech company is testing whether a new website optimization technique reduces the average page load time compared to their current method. To analyze this, they measure the load times (in milliseconds) for a random sample of web pages using the old and new techniques. Use the data below to perform a hypothesis test at the 1% significance level to test whether the new optimization technique leads to a lower average page load time.

